item.title: Popular pastime sending more Americans to ER with devastating injuries
item.description: Detroit-area doctors report a spike in e-bike crash injuries as Class 3 bikes reaching 28 mph cause major trauma among inexperienced riders.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit, Michigan, metro area is reporting an uptick in serious incidents related to electric bikes (e-bikes).

Fox 2 Detroit reported that police are seeing a rise in e-bike crashes, while doctors say they're treating a growing number of related injuries.

These incidents have reportedly led some communities to seek restrictions on e-bikes or to ban them altogether.

SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA

Some e-bikes can reach speeds of up to 28 miles per hour, increasing the potential severity of crashes on sidewalks and streets.

Fox 2 Detroit spoke with emergency room doctor Robert Sherwin of the Detroit Medical Center, who reported seeing everything from minor injuries to major trauma related to e-bike incidents.

"These Class 3 bikes are probably more like motor vehicles," he said. "They travel up to 28 miles an hour, and a lot of riders aren't expecting that, might not be experienced in that."

"These e-bikes are heavier than regular bikes, and they travel much faster, but the human body doesn't change just because a bike has a motor."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Fox 2 Detroit also spoke with local bike shop owner John Hughes, who suggested the "real issue" has always been sharing the road with cars.

"Cars aren't looking out for bikes ... people don't respect bikes as a form of transportation, and that's where it gets dangerous."

Hughes continued, "There's a ton of traffic out there. Everyone is on their cell phones. They're texting and driving constantly."

E-bike rider Cam Cason told Fox 2 Detroit that he takes his e-bike to work and school, crediting it as a "very efficient way" to get around.

"Way better than a car, in my opinion," he said. "When you don't have to spend $30 or $40 just to get some gas, use the electric bike to get where you need to go."

TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

As concerns over e-bike safety grow nationwide, states are beginning to tighten regulations. In New Jersey, a new law enacted this year requires e-bikes to be registered, and riders must be at least 15 years old and possess either a valid driver's license or an e-bike license to operate one.

The law was enacted amid growing concerns about e-bike crashes, including the death of a New Jersey teenager. Supporters argued that licensing, helmet and registration requirements would promote responsible riding and reduce bodily harm.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

NYU Langone Health released an advisory in April on the surge in brain and spine injuries related to e-bikes and scooters among riders and pedestrians in New York City.

According to a study published in the journal Neurosurgery, medical emergencies involving pedal-powered and electric bikes and scooters accounted for nearly 7% of trauma patients admitted to NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue.

One-third of the 914 patients treated for injuries involving pedal-powered and electric bikes and scooters suffered a traumatic brain injury. More than two-thirds required hospital admission and about 30% needed intensive care.

Physical harm linked to electric bikes and scooters increased from less than 10% of cases in 2018 to more than half by 2023, according to the study. The most common cause of injury, accounting for about half of all cases, was a collision with a car or truck.

Fewer than one-third of riders wore helmets, which was linked to a "significantly higher rate" of brain and facial injuries. The study found that 20% of patients tested positive for alcohol, which was associated with more severe head trauma and lower rates of helmet use.

Pedestrians struck by electric vehicles suffered brain injuries at nearly twice the rate of riders, according to an analysis of 69 pedestrian cases.

Corresponding author Hannah Weiss, MD, a resident in the Department of Neurosurgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, commented in a statement that these findings suggest "micromobility injuries are producing serious brain and spinal trauma that demands neurosurgical care at a scale we haven’t seen before."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"In a busy urban setting, we are seeing more and more of these injuries firsthand," she went on. "The data point to actionable solutions – helmet use, safer bike lane design and enforcement – that could prevent many of these injuries and better protect both riders and pedestrians."

Paul P. Huang, MD, associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and chief of neurosurgery at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue, added that the study highlights that "urban infrastructure must continue to improve to keep pace with the rapid rise of electric bikes and scooters."

"Future studies should track these injuries across multiple cities and measure whether protected bike lanes, helmet programs and speed enforcement actually reduce the number of brain and spine surgeries we perform," Huang said.

item.title: CNN panelist blames 'culture war' retribution as reason for Ryan Clark's ESPN departure
item.description: A CNN contributor claims Ryan Clark got swept up in culture war retribution, questioning how OutKick obtained the ESPN firing information early.
item.content:encoded:
Ryan Clark is no longer employed by ESPN.

After it was first reported by OutKick that Clark would be among a collection of on-air talents let go by the four-letter network Tuesday, July 21, the story shifted focus to a combination of cause and blame around the situation, and not the termination itself.

Clark was told the news on Monday during a taping of ESPN's 'NFL Live' after OutKick had obtained the information and had asked the network for comment. ESPN acted in such a manner, telling Clark during a taping, in an attempt to keep OutKick's Dan Zaksheske and Bobby Burack from breaking the story.

SPORTS MEDIA RUSHES TO CAST RYAN CLARK AS VICTIM WHILE PORTRAYING ESPN AS THE VILLAIN

In his first public comments following his ouster, Clark accused ESPN of intentionally leaking the news to OutKick. The fact that OutKick obtained the information hasn't exactly sat right with at least one CNN contributor.

During 'CNN This Morning' on Sunday, Jason "Jah" Lee raised questions about the situation as a whole while also pointing to Clark getting caught up in a "culture war" leading to his demise at ESPN.

"I think Ryan Clark got swept up in some level of culture war retribution," Lee, the senior editor at Bossip, explained. "The reason he got fired during the segment is because an outlet called OutKick contacted ESPN threatening to leak this information. How would OutKick get this information?

"OutKick is owned by Fox News Corp and was established by Clay Travis. If you know Clay Travis, he is not a bleeding-heart liberal. I feel a lot of this was purposefully done to embarrass Ryan Clark. ESPN has taken a lot of heat for being a liberal bastion lately, and I feel like perhaps [Clark's] bosses thought this was a time to push the other direction."

Clark, a former Super Bowl champion with the Pittsburgh Steelers, began his NFL analyst career at ESPN in 2015. According to Burack, he made around $2 million per year, roughly four times what the average NFL analyst earns.

item.title: TikTok influencer who accused estranged husband of pedophilia found dead in possible murder-suicide
item.description: Sara Gilson filed a protective order against Jeremiah Shawn Duffy weeks before police found both dead from apparent gunshot wounds in their Owasso home.
item.content:encoded:
TikTok influencer Sara Gilson, also known as Sara Duffey, posted weeks ago alleging that her husband was a pedophile. The estranged couple has since been found shot to death in the woman's Oklahoma home in what is reportedly believed to have been a murder-suicide.

Gilson, who had recently filed a protective order against her husband, 48-year-old Jeremiah "Shawn" Duffey, posted the TikTok video on July 11. It was captioned, "Preparing for when Netflix drops a documentary about my soon to be ex husband who I just found out is a pedophile." The video was still visible on her account as of Saturday.

Thirteen days after she posted that video, police reportedly responded to a domestic call on July 24 at 41-year-old Gilson's home. When officers arrived, they found Gilson and Duffey dead from apparent gunshot wounds, according to local outlet KTUL.

FORMER DEM VIRGINIA LT. GOV. KILLS WIFE, HIMSELF IN SHOCKING MURDER-SUICIDE: POLICE

KTUL cited an extended family member who identified the pair as the dead bodies in the home and said that Jeremiah, who went by Shawn, allegedly broke into the home, killed Sara and then himself. Police confirmed the couple's identities, according to local outlet KRMG, but did not say if it was a murder-suicide.

Police insisted there was no threat to the public at this time, according to KRMG.

HOUSTON RESTAURATEUR SUSPECTED OF KILLING PREGNANT WIFE AND TWO CHILDREN BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE

Authorities also said that the 911 call came from a juvenile in the house, the local media outlets reported.

Duffey had been ordered to stay at least 100 yards away from Gilson as part of her June 10 protective order against him.

On the same day she filed her protective order, another woman filed for a separate protective order against Duffey after he was allegedly spotted "kissing and fondling" her 15-year-old daughter, who played on the youth basketball team Duffey coached, according to The Oklahoman.

TEACHER WHO SERVED AS GOP STATE LAWMAKER ALLEGEDLY USED ROBLOX TO LURE STUDENT INTO SEXUAL RELATIONSHIP

Duffey had allegedly been sending the girl inappropriate messages and had given her money "to keep her quiet," the outlet reported.

After the coach was allegedly spotted with the girl, a report had been filed to the Owasso Police Department.

Gilson had also filed two previous protective orders against Duffey, though both were dismissed after Gilson failed to appear at the hearings, People reported.

Gilson and Duffey had reportedly shared children of their own.

Fox News Digital contacted the Owasso Police Department for confirmation and further details.

item.title: This red state is strengthening its grip as America's next economic heavyweight
item.description: IRS migration data reveal over $5 billion in wealth flowing into Texas as Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Austin fuel the state's population boom.
item.content:encoded:
The race to become America's next economic heavyweight may already have a frontrunner.

The latest Internal Revenue Service (IRS) migration data show billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into Texas, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth, strengthening a decades-long shift in America's economic center of gravity.

What's more, Texas isn't relying on a single boomtown. Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

That unusual breadth gives Texas multiple engines of economic growth, providing businesses with larger labor pools, diversified industries and a broader customer base than states anchored by a single dominant city.

BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES

The population boom has been accompanied by an influx of wealth. IRS migration data analyzed by the Tax Foundation show the Lone Star State gained more than $5 billion in adjusted gross income from interstate movers, while California and New York recorded multibillion-dollar losses.

"Capital follows where there is confidence," Texas Association of Business Chief Policy Officer Gabriela von zur Muehlen previously told Fox News Digital. "And right now there is a tremendous amount of confidence in Texas."

Von zur Muehlen said Texas' tax structure and predictable regulatory environment continue to attract businesses and investment from other states, helping reinforce the state's economic momentum.

While Florida attracted the nation's largest influx of taxpayer wealth and South Carolina posted the strongest inbound migration rate, Texas stood out by combining billions in new taxable income with rapid growth across Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio.

Economists say that combination matters because higher-income households bring spending, investment, entrepreneurship and tax revenue that can accelerate job creation, fuel commercial development and attract even more businesses. Over time, those forces can transform fast-growing metros into some of the nation's most influential economic hubs.

ONE SOUTHERN CITY YOU'VE NEVER HEARD OF IS GROWING FASTER THAN ANYWHERE ELSE IN AMERICA

Unlike simple population counts, adjusted gross income offers a glimpse into the economic resources newcomers bring with them. Higher-income households can contribute disproportionately to consumer spending, investment and local tax collections, making income migration an important measure of a region's long-term economic strength.

The migration data are only part of the story.

Earlier federal estimates showed Texas wasn't just adding residents — it was becoming wealthier on a per-person basis. Despite adding roughly 419,000 residents in 2025, more than any other state, Texas' economic output climbed to about $2.9 trillion, while per-capita GDP continued to rise, suggesting the state's economy was becoming more productive rather than simply larger.

THE RED STATES RACING AHEAD IN AMERICA'S POWERFUL WEALTH BOOM — AND THE STATES FALLING BEHIND

Business leaders say those trends are creating a self-reinforcing cycle. As more workers and higher-income households relocate to Texas, companies gain access to a larger labor pool and customer base, encouraging additional hiring, investment and expansion. That growth, in turn, creates more jobs and opportunities that can attract even more residents.

The migration has coincided with years of corporate relocations and business investment across the state, particularly in technology, finance, manufacturing and energy. The influx has also fueled new housing developments, logistics hubs, manufacturing projects and expanding commercial corridors across many of Texas' fastest-growing metropolitan areas.

Supporters of Texas' economic model argue its lack of a state income tax, relatively affordable cost of living and business-friendly climate continue attracting both employers and workers, reinforcing the state's long-term growth.

California and New York remain among the nation's largest and most influential economies.

But the latest Census, IRS and federal economic data suggest Texas continues gaining ground by attracting people, taxpayer wealth and economic output simultaneously, an uncommon combination that could reshape where businesses invest, jobs are created, and economic influence grows over the coming decade.

item.title: Black bears invade Lake Tahoe homes as break-ins surge and locals fortify defenses
item.description: Lake Tahoe homeowners are spending thousands on electric mats, reinforced doors and other bear deterrents as black bear break-ins surge this year.
item.content:encoded:
Black bears are increasingly breaking into homes around Lake Tahoe, leaving residents to spend thousands of dollars protecting their properties from hungry wildlife.

So far this year, South Lake Tahoe police have received 174 bear-related calls, compared with 97 during the same period last year, according to The Wall Street Journal. Several incidents involved bears making their way into homes.

One local couple told the publication they were washing dishes when they looked up to find a bear standing in their living room.

HIDDEN DANGER AT POPULAR US NATIONAL PARK FORCES TRAIL CLOSURES AS BEAR SIGHTINGS CLIMB

The animal wandered through the house, sniffed a tube of toothpaste in the bathroom and urinated on the floor before leaving. It was the couple's second bear break-in within the span of a month, the publication said.

As encounters become more common, some homeowners have begun installing electric mats, reinforced doors and other deterrents that can cost thousands of dollars.

Resident Margaret Deanesly Ziegler has installed everything from electric deterrents to a steel door to protect her summer cabin from bears, spending about $7,500 in the process, WSJ reported.

"I heard the most god-awful noise," the retired physician told the publication. "I heard the house being wrenched, the wood being torn apart."

"The bears are winning," Ziegler said. "I'm the one that's spending the money."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Similar encounters have occurred across the Lake Tahoe Basin in recent weeks.

Fox News Digital previously reported that a California man deployed bear spray after a black bear charged toward him outside his vacation home over the Fourth of July holiday. He spotted the animal rummaging through a garbage can inside his garage.

Video of the encounter captured the bear rushing toward the homeowner before he deployed the spray, sending the animal running away.

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife notes on its website that black bears are "highly food-motivated" and naturally investigate attractive smells in search of food.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The department recommends eliminating food attractants and blocking access to them with bear-proof containers, electric fencing or electric mats. It also warns that bears accustomed to human food can become increasingly bold and destructive, while cubs often learn those behaviors from their mothers.

The increase in encounters has also sparked debate among Lake Tahoe residents over whether bears or people are driving the problem.

"We don't have a bear problem, we have a people problem," one Reddit user wrote.

Another resident shared that a bear broke into their home earlier this year despite keeping trash secured, writing that they eventually installed bear mats because "it's just the price we pay to live side by side with bears."

Others said bears have remained a routine part of life around Lake Tahoe and that conflicts can often be avoided.

"Bears have been fine in my neighborhood," one user wrote. "Don't leave food or trash out and they just wander through."

Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Mamdani's politics linked to Muslim Brotherhood ideology as New York violence escalates: report
item.description: ISGAP research traces Zohran Mamdani's ties to Muslim Brotherhood-linked organizations as antisemitic violence escalates on Manhattan streets.
item.content:encoded:
On Tisha B'Av, the saddest day in the Jewish calendar marking the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem and the long history of catastrophes that followed, an assailant armed with a knife walked up to two men on Manhattan's Upper West Side and stabbed them. One wore a yarmulke.

Witnesses said the assailant shouted, "Allahu Akbar." The victims, ages 50 and 57, survived. A suspect is in custody, and police are examining the motive. But New York City did not need to wait for a formal designation to understand the gravity of the crime that had been perpetrated.

Only a day earlier, Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of the city with the largest Jewish community in the Diaspora, released a video accusing Israel of war crimes and genocide — and declared that Benjamin Netanyahu, the elected leader of the region's only democracy, should be arrested.

SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK

The mayor of an American city has no such power. Municipal leaders are forbidden by law from carrying out their own foreign policy. Nevertheless, Mamdani’s public relations stunt, amplified not only on social media but by the media of record, used language decrying the Jewish state as a criminal enterprise and suggesting that its defenders are fair game, setting the stage for bloodshed.

Jewish organizations had warned that the climate in the city was becoming dangerous. Their prescient warnings became prophetic as police officers cleaned up the crime scene.

It would not be appropriate to claim that any politician placed the weapon in the hands of the man who allegedly stabbed two innocent New Yorkers while attempting to terrorize the American Jewish community.

JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES

I contend something far more uncomfortable and dangerous: words and ideas lead to such actions, and a public culture that brands the Jewish state as genocidal or apartheid and treats "resistance" as a virtue normalizes a permission structure — in the dockets of justice and in the halls of power — in which such violence becomes thinkable.

This is the argument of a report that the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism & Policy (ISGAP) published on Mamdani in 2025. It is the argument that the events of this week have tragically underscored.

The report traces the origins of Mamdani’s worldview. As a student at Bowdoin College, Mamdani co-founded a chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine. In the aftermath of Oct. 7 — the largest single-day massacre of Jews since the Holocaust — he downplayed the atrocity while characterizing Israel's legally justified defensive response as genocide.

FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER DEFENDS HIMSELF FROM ANTISEMITISM ACCUSATIONS IN INTERVIEW WITH JEWISH OUTLET

He repeatedly declined to condemn the slogan "globalize the intifada," offering only that he would "discourage" its use, as though a call to export anti-Jewish violence to the streets of America were merely a matter of etiquette. He introduced legislation to punish New York charitable institutions that support Israel. His first act as mayor, before addressing police unions and garbage collection, was to remove the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism from the city’s lexicon.

He accepted a $100,000 donation from the Council on American-Islamic Relations, an organization identified by federal prosecutors as an unindicted co-conspirator in a terrorism-financing case, and he has associated with figures such as Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who served as a character witness for the man convicted of masterminding the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

These are not stray data points. His close friend, influencer Hasan Piker, and political candidates Mamdani has openly endorsed assert that the United States deserved what it got on Sept. 11, 2001 — a travesty as we prepare to honor the 25th anniversary of the attack on New York City itself. Mamdani’s words and actions form a dangerous pattern, and that pattern has a name: the Muslim Brotherhood.

ISGAP research on the Brotherhood's strategic entryism into North America describes a century-long campaign that its own internal documents lay out plainly. "The Project" of 1982 and the "Explanatory Memorandum" of 1991 — evidence entered in federal court — describe a strategy the authors call "civilization jihad": to exploit the freedoms of Western democracies to hollow them out from within, patiently, over generations, until the host society no longer recognizes what has been done to it.

Front organizations advise governments, shape civil-rights policy, embed themselves in universities and cultivate media, all while presenting a moderate face. Qatar underwrites much of it. Students for Justice in Palestine and American Muslims for Palestine sit within this ecosystem, and Hamas, which calls itself the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood and which the U.S. has designated a foreign terrorist organization, is what the ideology produces.

The Brotherhood is Sunni; the revolutionary regime in Tehran is Shia. On almost everything else, they are rivals, yet they converge on one project: the destruction of Israel and the humiliation of the West. When an American mayoral candidate adopts the same moral and political map, in which Israel is the aggressor and its enemies are the aggrieved, he is not dissenting bravely from consensus. He is translating a dangerous ideology into the fluent, sympathetic idiom of Western progressivism, where it does its most effective work precisely because it no longer seems foreign.

This is why the antisemitism at the center of Mamdani's politics cannot be waved away as a mere progressive ideology. Antisemitism is the oldest early-warning system a society has. It begins with Jews, and it never ends there. The same worldview that marks Jews as obstacles also marks pluralism, free exchange and the liberal democratic order itself as enemies. An assault on the Jews of New York is an assault on the idea of New York, on the essence of the American democratic experiment.

Listen closely to how Mamdani talks about his own city. The wealthy, landlords and the "billionaire class," in his telling, are a shadowy few who hoard the city and lock everyone else out. The language is reminiscent of Der Sturmer and the films produced by Joseph Goebbels. Presented as economic justice, this is familiar and dangerous rhetoric.

The oldest antisemitic libels have always relied on the image of a rich, rootless minority pulling the strings while ordinary people suffer. When a politician's economic populism runs on the same rails as his hostility toward the Jewish state, the two are not unrelated. They draw from the same well. This is why the assault is not merely on Jews or Israel. It is on the very fabric of the U.S. — on the idea that a free society is built through commerce, contract, and pluralism rather than resentment, expropriation and the search for an enemy within.

A man was knifed outside a synagogue on the saddest day of the Jewish year in a city whose mayor spends his energy accusing the Jewish state of genocide. We must say clearly what connects the rhetoric to the risk, refuse the normalization of hatred dressed up as social justice, and insist that words that prepare the ground for violence be named for what they are before the next knife is drawn.

Unrestrained by his theatrical and ineffectual call for Netanyahu’s arrest, Mamdani now calls for massive demonstrations when the Israeli leader visits the city for the U.N. General Assembly in September.

"The mayor’s activist posturing puts police officers on the street in a terrible position," New York City Police Benevolent Association President Patrick Hendry said. "Protests during the U.N. General Assembly are nothing new, but when the mayor of the city is actively calling for demonstrations, violent agitators will assume they have permission to cause as much havoc as possible."

The stabbings in Manhattan are just the beginning of something far more dangerous. Mamdani, it appears, has sounded the call, content that the globalization of the intifada will erupt on the streets of the city he is sworn to serve.

item.title: Christopher Sanchez's dominant home ERA makes Phillies run line the play against Yankees
item.description: Will Warren takes the mound as the Yankees seek a sweep, but Christopher Sanchez's dominant 1.03 home ERA makes the Phillies run line enticing.
item.content:encoded:
It was a bit of a dull weekend on the diamond. I haven't been all that impressed with the matchups. Usually, baseball has some really good pairings for the weekend, but now and then, there aren't too many impressive series. I do like the Seattle and Texas one, but we've covered them once, and I don't have a great read on the game today. So, I'm going with the other game that I like - New York vs. Philadelphia.

The New York Yankees are just two games back in their division, but for whatever reason, it feels like this team is on the verge of a collapse. Maybe I'm exaggerating here, but something about the conversation from the media is that the Yankees are falling apart. I don't quite see it, but they do have a very talented roster on the injured list, so maybe that's the issue. The good news for them is that Ben Rice is having a fantastic season, their players could all return healthy in plenty of time, and they are still a likely playoff team.

The Yankees are looking for a sweep today, and they send out Will Warren to get the job done. Warren has been fine this year. He has been reliable, tossed a reasonable number of innings, and hasn't missed any time due to injury. He did, for some reason, pitch for less than an inning in relief on Wednesday. His numbers are seven wins and four losses, with a 4.00 ERA and a 1.37 WHIP. Philadelphia hitters have seen him 31 times and gotten eight hits, with only Kyle Schwarber launching one over the fence.

AARON JUDGE OFFICIALLY OUT INDEFINITELY WITH STRESS FRACTURE IN HUGE BLOW TO YANKEES' TITLE HOPES

The Philadelphia Phillies have been one of the better teams in baseball this season. They are 5.5 games back of the Braves at the moment, but this was a division that looked like Atlanta would lock up by the end of May, so this has been some progress. Looking at the team and players' statistics, the one thing that has stood out to me is that Schwarber leads them in homers, Brandon Marsh leads in average, and Bryce Harper leads in RBIs. It isn't just that three different guys lead them in three different categories; it is that there are even more on the team having really strong years. They have six guys hitting .240 or better.

It shouldn't be surprising that a good team has players performing well. Part of what makes the Phillies so dangerous is their ability to not need just one guy to carry the load. In the rotation, I will say one guy, tonight's starter, does seem to be carrying his weight and then some. Christopher Sanchez is having another solid year with a 12-4 record, 2.64 ERA, and a 1.19 WHIP. Sanchez has been fantastic at home with a 1.03 ERA as well. Honestly, the only bad home start he has had was the All-Star Game. Yankees hitters are hitting just .200 against him in 45 at-bats.

I'm sure we can find a player prop if you're looking for that sort of thing. Ever since sports betting became legal basically everywhere, I feel like the daily fantasy stuff is not as popular. Maybe it is, and I'm just not paying attention. Either way, Cody Bellinger is someone you might want to add on the team, and Ryan McMahon is someone to fade.

For the game, there are two options here - the Phillies, despite losing the first two games of this series, should win tonight. Sanchez has been great in Philadelphia. Paying -193 for them to win is not something I'm interested in. Instead, I am going to take the Phillies on the Run Line tonight. I've made this point before and need to follow it more. The Yankees have had 25 1-run games this year, and the Phillies have had 27. In 105 games, that's less than 25% of their final scores being decided by a run. Give me the Phillies -1.5.

item.title: Everyday Revolutionary War heroes take center stage in Trump's 'Spirit of '76' exhibit
item.description: The Caesar Rodney statue and 22 other installations at Freedom Plaza honor common, everyday Revolutionary War heroes as part of America's 250th anniversary under President Trump.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Beneath a towering 23-foot bronze figure holding the Declaration of Independence aloft, designer Matthew Taylor stopped beside an equestrian statue that many Americans have likely never seen, or even heard of.

"Most Americans have never heard of Caesar Rodney," Taylor told Fox News Digital during an exclusive tour of the new Spirit of '76 exhibition at Freedom Plaza. "But we owe this man an enormous debt of gratitude."

The temporary installation, unveiled as part of America's 250th anniversary celebration, transforms Freedom Plaza into an open-air gallery honoring Revolutionary War figures whose names rarely appear in history textbooks.

Commissioned by President Donald Trump, the exhibition features 22 statues and sculptural installations, including a restored equestrian monument of Rodney, a towering "Spirit of Liberty" centerpiece, bronze figures representing Revolutionary soldiers, and an immersive memorial honoring Americans who died aboard British prison ships during the Revolution.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

According to the National Park Service, the exhibit was created to honor the "heroes and martyrs of the Revolution" during America's semiquincentennial and is intended to celebrate the enduring "Spirit of '76' that continues to live on in every American heart." 

The centerpiece installations include the Caesar Rodney equestrian statue, the "12 Soldiers of the Revolution," the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial and the 23-foot Spirit of Liberty statue.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL DIG AT BATTLE OF BUNKER HILL SITE UNCOVERS REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS

Rather than beginning with George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, however, Taylor chose to introduce visitors to Rodney.

The Delaware statesman, one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence, is remembered for his legendary overnight ride from Dover to Philadelphia in July 1776. Suffering from severe illness, Rodney rode roughly 80 miles through a storm to cast the vote that broke Delaware's deadlock in favor of independence.

"Of all the signers of the Declaration of Independence, Caesar Rodney is one of the most exciting," Taylor said. "When Delaware's delegation was deadlocked, he rode through the night to cast the vote that helped secure American independence."

THE REVOLUTIONARY LANDMARKS WHERE WASHINGTON, ADAMS AND JEFFERSON CHANGED AMERICA

For decades, the bronze statue stood in Wilmington's Rodney Square before being removed in 2020. It now occupies one of the most prominent locations in the nation's capital, just blocks from both the White House and the Capitol.

From Rodney's ride, Taylor naturally guides visitors into the next chapter of the American story.

Arranged around the plaza are bronze sculptures representing 12 Revolutionary War soldiers. Rather than depicting famous generals, the statues celebrate ordinary Americans whose individual stories reflect the sacrifices of the Revolutionary generation.

"These are ordinary citizens who did extraordinary things," Taylor said. "Every one of these statues tells the story of someone who answered the call during the Revolution."

Among them is Samuel Whittemore, who fought British troops at age 78. According to Taylor, Whittemore was bayoneted multiple times, shot in the head and left for dead before surviving and living into his 90s.

Another figure, Simon Knowles, enlisted at just 15 years old and served alongside George Washington throughout much of the Revolutionary War before returning home to live as a farmer.

Taylor said those stories represent the exhibition's central message.

"Unlike monuments to George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, these statues honor ordinary Americans who did extraordinary things," he said.

Nearby, another installation tells one of the Revolution's lesser-known tragedies.

Designed as visitors physically walk through its narrow bronze panels, the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial recreates the outline of a British prison ship. According to the National Park Service, nearly 12,000 Americans died aboard prison ships during the Revolutionary War; even more than were killed in combat during the conflict.

Taylor said the memorial is meant to immerse visitors in that experience.

"As you walk inside, you hear the water from the fountain," he explained during the tour. "It helps place you inside the story."

The fountain itself has also become part of the experience. Taylor noted it was recently restored to operation after years of sitting idle, providing the soundscape surrounding the memorial while complementing the plaza's redesign.

Towering above the entire exhibition stands the Spirit of Liberty, a new bronze figure inspired by iconic American monuments while looking toward the country's next 250 years.

Standing 23 feet tall, the statue holds an exact bronze replica of the Declaration of Independence in one hand while raising a sword skyward with the other. Around its base are reliefs depicting three defining moments of the Revolution: the signing of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington crossing the Delaware River and the British surrender at Yorktown.

"The Spirit of Liberty represents the sacrifices that gave birth to this nation," Taylor said.

During Fox News Digital's visit, visitors gathered around the plaza to photograph the statues against the Washington skyline. Low-angle views of the bronze figures framed them against bright summer skies, while Rodney's horse appeared frozen mid-stride as though continuing the historic ride that helped shape the nation's founding.

For Taylor, whose career has largely been spent both behind the camera and behind the scenes designing historical works, the exhibition is about more than commemorating famous names.

Instead, he hopes visitors leave thinking about people they had never encountered before arriving at Freedom Plaza.

"When visitors leave here," Taylor said, "I hope they realize they can do extraordinary things themselves. America was built by ordinary citizens who answered extraordinary moments."

The Spirit of '76 exhibition is free to the public and is scheduled to remain on display throughout the nation's 250th anniversary celebration.

item.title: Los Angeles Rams betting outlook: why one analyst is all in on a Super Bowl win at +550
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams added Myles Garrett via trade and bolstered their secondary, but questions remain about Matthew Stafford and Aaron Donald's future.
item.content:encoded:
If you watched the Super Bowl last year, you were probably a bit disappointed. I’m sure you weren’t if you were a Seahawks fan, and I know that I was happy about some of the outcomes, but the game itself was a bit boring. That was a lot different than the NFC Championship game, which was a fantastic back-and-forth battle between the Seahawks and the team we break down here, the Rams.

Last Year

As mentioned, the Los Angeles Rams made it to the NFC Championship before falling short against the Seahawks. It was a good run, but the Rams did look vulnerable in each of their playoff games. They started against the Panthers and seemed like they were going to lose until they had some Matthew Stafford heroics. Speaking of Stafford, he ended up with one of the best seasons of his career and the MVP award. In the Divisional Playoffs, he capitalized on a bad route or bad throw (depending on who you ask) from the Bears and stole a 20-17 overtime win. He was great against the Seahawks, but the Rams defense couldn’t get a stop.

REIGNING MVP MATTHEW STAFFORD LOCKS IN EXTENSION WITH RAMS WORTH UP TO $60M WITH INCENTIVES

Offseason additions and subtractions

That inability to get a stop may be part of the reason that Los Angeles went out and made a major splash this offseason. They traded for Myles Garrett, arguably the best defensive player on the planet at the moment. It was so big that even Aaron Donald is considering coming back to the team, and out of retirement. Stafford is coming back after contemplating retirement, so they shored up that concern. They added Trent McDuffie, one of the better cornerbacks in the league, and grabbed Jaylen Watson from free agency to address the other side of their secondary. Their defense should be even better.

Roster

If Donald comes out of retirement, he probably won’t be quite as elite as he was in the past, but I have to imagine he is still in shape and would be ready by the time the season starts. It doesn’t look like he is coming, though. Still, this defense, which was solid but not great last season, could be amazing this season. I don’t know that Stafford will lead the league in touchdowns and yards, but he still has Davante Adams and Puka Nacua. If his offensive line protects him and gives him time, he will carve up even the best defenses he faces.

Betting Outlook

I am all in on the Rams this year. I think they are the best team in the NFL and have very few exploitable weaknesses. They are in a tough division – the Seahawks will still be good, the 49ers are always a tough team – but I think 11.5 wins is an over for them. I have them at 13 wins for the year. I also like them to win the Super Bowl at +550. Maybe I’m overconfident in their defense with Garrett or a 38-year-old quarterback, but I think the Rams have all the pieces and will close the deal this season.

item.title: Witness recounts Fourth of July weekend Bigfoot sighting in Connecticut, says 'there were no boobs'
item.description: A man claims he saw an 8-foot-tall Bigfoot cross the road in Voluntown, Connecticut, while driving home to Rhode Island after the Fourth of July.
item.content:encoded:
In the early morning hours of July 5, a man saw a Bigfoot shortly after leaving a cabin a friend of his had rented in Voluntown, Connecticut, presumably for the Fourth of July weekend. The man was making his way back home to Rhode Island at the time.

After leaving the cabin's long dirt driveway and crossing a bridge on the road, he wrote to The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization that he "witnessed something jump into the road from my right heading to the woods on my left."

He had to hit his brakes so that he wouldn’t hit the "bipedal, 8-8½ foot tall creature." The presumed Bigfoot didn’t stop and never looked at him as it crossed the road in front of him.

TWO LADIES, A DOG, A LIGHTHOUSE AND A POSSIBLE BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER ON A BEACH IN MICHIGAN

"It had coarse, matted, and greasy looking long brown hair covering every part of its body I could see," wrote the witness who went on camera with an investigator a few days after the sighting.

"Its legs were shorter than its torso and its arms literally hung down to right around knee height. Must have had an 8 - 9ft 'wing span' if it fully outstretched its arms."

He was a skeptic before the sighting, but is not a skeptic anymore. It took him "a minimum of 60-90 seconds to regain control of my faculties" and continue his drive home.

BIGFOOT IS A NEANDERTHAL-HUMAN HYBRID, ACCORDING TO THE MAN WHO CLAIMS TO HAVE FOUND REMAINS

This wasn't a bear caught in his high beams, he insists. It was a cryptid that walked in front of his car. That he is certain of. He spoke to two BFRO investigators and went on camera from the spot where he claims to have seen the Bigfoot.

While recalling his sighting, he was asked if he thought the Bigfoot he saw was male or female. He responded, "I, you know, I don't know... I'll say this, if the females are that big, I don't want to see a male."

Someone off camera, we can assume from the response he gave, asked if the Bigfoot he saw had boobs. The witness replied, "No, there were no boobs."

Sometimes you have to ask the tough questions. Are we any closer to knowing the truth about Bigfoot based on this sighting?

I don't think we can answer that. Not at the moment anyway.

However, as long as we have people out there willing to investigate reports and ask the questions no one else is willing to, that includes whether the Bigfoot had boobs or not, we're headed in the right direction.

item.title: 'Shark Week' host Forrest Galante explains why crushing beers in the ocean is a bad idea
item.description: Forrest Galante shares simple shark safety tips ahead of his Discovery special, from avoiding dawn swims to why crushing a beer can underwater is risky.
item.content:encoded:
It’s the most wonderful time of the year: "Shark Week."

That annual stretch when Americans collectively gather around their TV sets to learn everything there is to know about the ocean’s apex predators and to ask ourselves why we are dumb enough to swim in the ocean in the first place.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

But lucky for those of us who don’t want to end up the subject of a future "Shark Week" documentary, wildlife biologist, conservationist and TV host Forrest Galante has some simple advice.

Galante recently joined OutKick Outdoors to talk about shark attacks, shark behavior and his upcoming Discovery special, "Alien Sharks: Untamed America." And while he stressed that the chances of having a negative shark encounter are already extremely slim, he said beachgoers can make those odds even better by using some common sense.

"You know, the best thing you can do is educate yourself," Galante said. "Think about where you're going. Learn what the species are."

If you are looking for some blanket rules before your next beach trip, Galante offered a few.

"Don't go in the water at dawn or dusk," Galante said.

Sharks are crepuscular, meaning they are most active at dawn and dusk. That is when they are more likely to be feeding closer to shore, which is also exactly where people tend to be splashing around during summer vacation.

"Don't swim near river mouths," Galante said. "That's when sharks are feeding."

River mouths can attract baitfish and other food sources, which can also attract sharks. If there is a place where sharks are naturally more likely to congregate, that is probably not the spot to float around with a drink in your hand and your guard down.

"Don't go swimming by yourself," Galante said.

This is one of those tips that applies to pretty much every outdoor activity. Hiking alone, boating alone, swimming alone — all of it adds risk.

And Galante said there is another simple clue beachgoers should pay attention to.

"If you see no one on the beach, that's usually not a good place to go swimming," he said.

"On the flip side of that, don't go swimming where people are fishing and throwing bait in the water and things like that," Galante said.

This one should be obvious, but apparently we need to say it anyway. If people are actively tossing shark food into the water, you can probably bet sharks will be there, too.

Sharks are not hunting humans, but they are curious predators. And sometimes, something as simple as a flash of light can get their attention.

"Wearing something highly shiny, like jewelry or sequins or anything with those little mirrors that put out light, can look like a school of bait fish," Galante said.

That matters because, according to Galante, shark attacks on humans are usually because the shark thinks you're something else.

"They say that something like 99% of shark bites are a case of mistaken identity," he said. "You see a flash from a sparkly bit of jewelry or something, and the shark goes, ‘Oh wow, is that food?’ Unfortunately, when a shark asks the question, ‘Is that food?’ they do so by taking an investigative bite."

FORREST GALANTE SAYS MOST SHARK BITES ARE A CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY AS FLORIDA ATTACKS LEAD THE US

And that is where things can go very wrong.

"They don't have hands," Galante said. "They can't feel it, so that investigative bite can be very, very damaging and, in some cases, fatal."

This is the one that might surprise people. According to Galante, even certain sounds can draw a shark's attention.

"The crackling of a water bottle, or even the crunching of a beer can, sounds a lot like the crunching of fish bones to a shark, and it can make them come and investigate," he said.

Galante made it clear that most sharks are not looking for humans as prey.

"Most of the time, we're not even on the menu," Galante said. "They're just trying to figure out if we are."

So no matter what horrors you see on your TV screen this week, there is no need to cancel your beach trip.

"Just taking a few very simple precautions can greatly reduce your already very slim chance of having a negative encounter," Galante said.

Galante’s Shark Week special, "Alien Sharks: Untamed America," premieres Wednesday on Discovery and Max. The special follows him across the United States in search of some of the strangest and least-known shark species living in American waters — including glow-in-the-dark swell sharks, seagrass-eating bonnethead sharks, massive basking sharks and sawfish that look like something out of Star Wars .

"We have some of the coolest, the largest, the smallest, the weirdest and the most bizarre and incredible sharks right here in the United States," Galante said.

Which is cool.

Just maybe don’t go looking for them at dusk while wearing sequins and crushing a beer can.

item.title: Melissa Gilbert, Michael Landon and more: Where the original 'Little House on the Prairie' cast is now
item.description: The Netflix reboot has sparked renewed interest in the 1974 series. Reconciliations, salary disputes and surprising career paths followed the cast.
item.content:encoded:
The popular new adaptation of "Little House on the Prairie," which began streaming on Netflix earlier this month, has caused a resurgence of interest in the original 1974 television series starring Melissa Gilbert and Michael Landon.

But what happened to the original cast?

Melissa Gilbert is best known for her portrayal of Laura Ingalls in the original series, which she began in 1974 at just 9 years old.

The 62-year-old had already been on shows like "Gunsmoke" and "Emergency" when the show started.

Also serving as the narrator of the show, Gilbert stayed on "Little House on the Prairie" for all nine seasons, until 1983.

BELOVED 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' FACES WAGONLOAD OF 'WOKE' ALLEGATIONS OVER NETFLIX REBOOT

During her time on the show, she made several TV movies, including "The Miracle Worker," "The Diary of Anne Frank" and "Splendor in the Grass."

She also reprised her role in the TV movies "Little House Years," "Little House: Look Back to Yesterday," "Little House: The Final Farewell" and "Little House: Bless All the Dear Children."

Gilbert continued to act after the show ended on dozens of TV movies and she also voiced Barbara Gordon on "Batman: The Animated Series" from 1992 to 1994.

Gilbert also made TV appearances on shows like "Touched by an Angel," "Providence," "7th Heaven" and "Nip/Tuck." She had a recurring role on Hallmark’s "When Calls the Heart," but recently revealed in an Instagram post that she would not be returning to the show. She said she was told that was due to "budget issues."

The news came after her husband Timothy Busfield, who she married in 2013, was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor and one count of child abuse in January. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a minor.

Busfield has denied the charges and Gilbert has continued to support him, telling ABC in April that he is the "last person in the world who would hurt a child."

"I trust him with my children's lives, with my grandchildren's lives, my nieces and nephews," she added. "He is an honorable, caring, generous human being."

ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE' VILLAIN RETURNS FOR REBOOT WITH WARNING FOR NEW NELLIE

Gilbert also defended the new reboot after she said she’d seen fans debating on social media whether the new version or the original were historically accurate and faithful to the books.

"The short answer is no, neither are entirely accurate to the times nor the books," she wrote in a Substack essay.

After giving several examples of inaccuracies, she wrote: "My hope is that folks realize that these are all perfect examples of dramatic license. Even the real Laura took dramatic license in writing her books. For example, in the book, ‘Little House on the Prairie,’ all three Ingalls girls are older than they were in real life."

She added, "So rather than getting all twisted up in what’s real and what’s dramatized, maybe just sit back and go for the ride the creative minds behind these shows want to take you on. If you like it, stick with it. If you don’t, you don’t have to watch."

Michael Landon, who played Laura’s father Charles Ingalls on the show, began acting in the 1950s, appearing on shows like "Cheyenne," "Suspicion" and "The Rifleman." He was also in the movie "I Was a Teenage Werewolf."

Landon directed many of the show’s episodes and wrote and produced the show.

Before "Little House," he starred as Little Joe Cartwright on the long-running series "Bonanza."

Landon continued to work on several TV movies after the show ended, and he starred as angel Jonathan Smith on the 1984 to 1989 series "Highway to Heaven."

He also reprised his role as Charles Ingalls in four TV movies.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Landon died at 54 years old in 1991, just months after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

Gilbert called Landon a "mentor and father figure" in a Fox News Digital interview in 2024. She said she saw her TV dad a week before he died.

"There were always funny moments with Michael," she said. "Even as sick as he was, he still maintained his incredible sense of humor."

Gilbert frequently posts memories of him on her Instagram, writing earlier this month, "I’ve always felt like the luckiest girl in the world because he chose me to be his ‘Halfpint.’ Working with him was more than formative. I learned most of what I know about our industry from him."

Karen Grassle, who played Laura’s mother Caroline, was mainly a theater and Broadway actress before landing the role on "Little House."

After the show ended, the 84-year-old continued to act until 2021, starring in the movie "Not to Forget."

Grassle had a contentious relationship with Landon while on the show, which stemmed from a salary dispute in Season 2 and prompted her to leave a year before the show ended.

She formed a special bond with her onscreen children "so they felt comfortable doing scenes with me as their mother," but her relationship with Landon, whom she called an "amazing, multi-talented person," soured, according to People magazine.

"I felt insulted as his co-star on a hit series," Grassle told the New York Post about his refusal to grant her a raise, arguing she should be paid the same as her onscreen children. "I didn’t want to gouge anybody, but I expected a fair wage."

She said Landon also cut her onscreen time during the dispute and made sexist jokes on set.

The actress reconciled with Landon before his death, telling the Post: "I am very grateful that we mended our fences."

Grassle is also very proud of her time on "Little House," calling her character "an incredibly strong woman with a nature full of texture. Her spirit is one to live by."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Melissa Sue Anderson played Laura’s older sister Mary Ingalls on the show.

The 63-year-old was the only member of the cast to be nominated for an Emmy for an episode about her character going blind.

Two years older than Gilbert when she started on the pioneer show, Anderson had only done a little TV work — including as Bobby Brady’s first kiss — before "Little House."

Anderson made her film debut in the horror movie "Happy Birthday to Me" in 1981 and after the show ended, she made TV appearances on shows like "Hotel," "Murder She Wrote," "The Equalizer" and "The Love Boat."

She met her husband, Michael Sloan, while appearing in the 1980s reprisal of "Alfred Hitchcock Presents." The couple welcomed two daughters and Sloan died in 2025.

Anderson and Gilbert famously didn’t get along.

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' RETURNS AS NEW NETFLIX ADAPTATION AIMS FOR WHOLESOME ENTERTAINMENT

"We were very, very different," Anderson told the Atlanta Constitution-Journal.

Anderson also published a memoir about her time on the show called "The Way I See It: A Look Back at My Life on Little House."

Gilbert felt that Anderson acted like the boss on set.

"From the moment we walked onto that set, Melissa Sue Anderson was the boss of me," she said in an interview, according to Parade. "She took that absolutely seriously. She was two years older than me, which, you know, when you’re 9 and 11 is a big deal."

Gilbert added, "She was tough on me both off and on camera, but on camera especially."

Anderson explained that she was just very shy, telling Harry Brownstone on his podcast last year: "I wish I had been more outgoing so I could have enjoyed it more and been more easygoing about everything."

However, the pair reunited last year at Gilbert’s off-Broadway play "Pen Pals."

"Reconnection with a sister," Gilbert wrote. "Long, healing talks. Lots of reminiscing. Lots of catching up. Lots of laughter and a few tears."

MICHAEL LANDON'S 'LITTLE HOUSE' CO-STAR EXPOSES ACTOR'S WILD ON-SET PRANKS

"Just us Ingalls girls. The best part is, the past is now just that and we can move forward as the sisters/friends we always wanted to be," she wrote.

Twins Rachel Lindsay and Sidney Greenbush were just 3 years old when they were cast as younger sister Carrie Ingalls.

Sharing the role for eight years, they chose to leave after the eighth season when they were 12 years old.

"Everybody separated, and I didn’t see anybody," Rachel Lindsay said at a 50th anniversary reunion, according to Entertainment Weekly. "And that was really hard for me personally because I didn’t realize how connected I had been to everybody until years later."

"You make these really deep, intense bonds working with each other every single day, and then when it’s over, you’re just supposed to be like, ‘Okay, that was nice. Bye,’" she told the outlet. "And it’s really hard that way."

Both sisters retired from acting in 1983 to focus on their education.

In 2014, she married Daniel Sanchez, whom she first met when he lived near the set and used to sneak on to hang out with the cast and crew, according to People magazine.

She also has a grown daughter from a previous relationship.

Sidney acted in "Hambone and Hillie" in 1983 and Rachel Lindsay was in an episode of "Matt Houston."

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR REVEALS WILD FRIENDSHIP WITH JIM MORRISON BEFORE WHOLESOME TV FAME

Sidney just wrote a children’s book called "Seven Sisters: The Lantern of Humanity."

"I remember when they were making the movie 'Return to Oz.' My sister made it to the final three girls who were selected," Sidney told Fox News Digital last month.

"They all did screen tests, and for the silliest of reasons, they chose another girl over her," she said. "Of course, we all know there can only be one choice in the end, but it's a lot of pressure for children. So I decided I was going to explore other things because sometimes you go to what they call 'cattle calls,' where there are so many people competing for the same role. The casting directors aren't always nice."

The two sisters were credited as "Lindsay Sidney Greenbush" on the show.

Nellie Oleson, the daughter of the mercantile store owners who bullied Laura, was played by Alison Arngrim.

The 64-year-old was just 12 when she began acting opposite Gilbert, saying at the 50th reunion the two of them were "like sisters" on set, according to People.

"It's so completely bonkers," Arngrim said. "Here's Melissa Gilbert and I playing mortal enemies, beating each other senseless all week. And then on the weekends, we'd go to each other's house for a slumber party, and we were hanging out."

She is also the author of "Confessions of A Prairie Bitch: How I Survived Nellie Oleson and Learned to Love Being Hated" and had a one-woman show called "Confessions of a Prairie Bitch."

In 2002, she was honored with the Young Artist Former Child Star Lifetime Achievement Award for her work on the show.

Aside from "Little House, Arngrim also made appearances on shows like "Fantasy Island," "The Love Boat," the TV movie "Life Interrupted" and she recently made a cameo on the "Little House" reboot.

Katherine MacGregor played nasty gossip Harriet Oleson on the show.

After she died at 93 years old in 2018, Gilbert called her "outspoken and hilariously funny" in an Instagram post.

"A truly gifted actress as she was able to play a despicable character but with so much heart. Her Harriet Oleson was the woman our fans loved to hate. A perfect antagonist," she added.

"The thing people outside of our prairie family didn't know, was how loving and nurturing she was with the younger cast."

Before "Little House," MacGregor acted on shows like "Mister Peepers," "Mannix," "Emergency!" "All in the Family" and "Ironside."

NETFLIX'S 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' ACTOR HOPES NEW SERIES WILL UNITE OLD AND NEW FANS

She was also a successful Broadway actress and she returned to the theater after the show ended. She retired from acting in the early 2000s.

Richard Bull played Nels Oleson, husband to Harriet who, with her, owned the town mercantile store.

Bull began acting in the 1950s, landing parts on shows like "Perry Mason," "Highway Patrol," "The Virginian," "The Fugitive," "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "Gidget," "Gomer Pyle: USMC," "The Andy Griffith Show," "Bewitched," "Mission: Impossible" and "Bonanza" before the show’s run.

He also starred as the doctor on "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea" from 1964 to 1968.

He continued to act until 2011 on shows like "Lou Grant," "Knots Landing," "Hillstreet Blues," "Designing Women" and "ER."

Bull died at 89 years old in 2014.

He also reunited with Landon on three episodes of "Highway to Heaven."

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

Dean Butler played Laura’s eventual husband, Almanzo Wilder, who came onto the show in the sixth season.

He also appeared on shows like "CHiPs," "Fantasy Island," "Who’s the Boss?" "The Love Boat," "Hotel," and had a recurring role on "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."

From 1986 until 1988, he starred on "The New Gidget" as Jeff "Moondoggie" Griffin.

His last acting role was in 2008, and since then he has mainly worked behind the camera as a sports, entertainment and documentary producer, including a docuseries he narrated called "The Little House Phenomenon: A Place in Television History."

Butler, like Gilbert, commended the reboot, writing on Instagram earlier this month: "Something that I love about the program that I think would have been really fun in the original — which we did not do... is the family singing. Writers have rolled in songs that Pa played on his fiddle, and the family is singing along, and they’re doing it beautifully, and this really is the spirit of Laura’s books."

He added that the show is beautifully produced, saying "there is a lot of good stuff going on here."

item.title: Fauci's newly released COVID diaries reveal bizarre fixation on fame as pandemic deaths mounted
item.description: Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal he called himself the most famous person in the country while documenting rising COVID-19 death tolls.
item.content:encoded:
Newly released diary entries reveal that as COVID-19 deaths mounted around the world, former White House COVID advisor Dr. Anthony Fauci became increasingly fixated on his newfound celebrity.

Released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., the journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, media appearances, and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded.

Paul, a longtime Fauci critic who frequently clashed with Fauci over the federal response and the origins of the virus, made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The release comes days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul.

GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION

A surprising recurring theme throughout the diaries is Fauci's growing awareness of his own public profile during the most intense months of the pandemic, which ultimately claimed more than 7 million officially reported lives worldwide, including roughly 1.2 million in the United States.

On April 7, 2020, after recording the latest pandemic developments, Fauci wrote: "Press still hot and heavy about me. Multiple stories per day directly or indirectly involving me."

SLACK MESSAGES RELEASED BY RAND PAUL APPEAR TO SHOW AUTHORS OF KEY COVID-19 ORIGIN PAPER HELD PRIVATE DOUBTS

By May 21, after recording the latest pandemic figures — nearly 98,000 global deaths and more than 27,000 U.S. deaths — and documenting the day's White House coronavirus task force meetings, Fauci wrote that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

He added that Trump "seems to be enamored of me even though I am taking the spotlight away from him," writing that the two were developing "a very unique and interesting relationship." Fauci also noted that Secret Service agents had become so familiar with him they often waved him through White House security without checking his identification.

As the attention continued to grow, the diary increasingly documented how Fauci's prominence had expanded beyond public health. A month later, as the United States recorded what Fauci described as a record 40,000 new COVID-19 cases in a single day, he wrote that he had been invited to appear on "Dancing with the Stars."

LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

The diaries also document Fauci's growing frustration with the Trump White House. On July 2, 2020, after warning that the country could be entering an "exponential" increase in COVID-19 cases heading into the Fourth of July weekend, Fauci wrote, "POTUS and his people have essentially dropped out and do not even recognize that an outbreak is ongoing."

He also complained that the White House was denying requests for him to appear on major television programs. Across multiple entries, Fauci criticized White House communications officials for restricting his television appearances, questioned the administration's public messaging and expressed frustration that media coverage increasingly portrayed him as being at odds with Trump.

ANTHONY FAUCI DELIVERED ONE OF THE WORST FIRST PITCHES IN BASEBALL HISTORY SIX YEARS AGO

Fauci also repeatedly defended himself against what he described as the "countless" profiles written about him. He wrote that White House officials were upset because the coverage made it appear he was becoming "a star that outshines" the president.

He also insisted several of the profiles had been written without interviewing him and wrote that he had "no desire to conflict with, embarrass or show up the POTUS," later deciding to stop participating in profile interviews altogether.

Taken together, the entries offer an unusually personal account of Fauci's role during one of the most consequential public health crises in modern U.S. history, capturing not only the government's internal deliberations but also his private concerns about the pandemic, his increasingly complicated relationship with the Trump White House and the extraordinary public attention that followed.

A suspect in the attack at Berlin's Pride festival that left one person dead and at least 29 others injured was killed during a confrontation with police in a nearby suburb, The Associated Press reported, citing authorities.

German authorities on Sunday launched an intensive manhunt for Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots. Ballout was killed following a nearly 24-hour search. Prosecutors said he had previously sought to join the militant Islamic State group.

"Everything we see here points to us dealing with an Islamic terror attack," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said.

AT LEAST 1 DEAD, SEVERAL INJURED AFTER VAN RAMS INTO CROWD AT PRIDE FESTIVAL; SUSPECT 'KNOWN TO POLICE'

The minister said the suspect had previously come to the attention of authorities for multiple crimes, as well as his "radicalization and belonging to the Islamist scene."

Dobrindt said Ballout was born in Germany and that his mother became a naturalized German citizen in 2002, three years before he was born. He said the suspect previously received a suspended prison sentence of one year and 10 months but did not disclose what he had been convicted of.

Police said a white van drove into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park around 10 p.m. on Saturday before crashing into a tree. Authorities say the suspect then attacked several people with a machete before fleeing.

WITNESSES RECOUNT 'SCARY' NYC STABBING AFTER SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY YELLED 'ALLAHU AKBAR' DURING ATTACKS

A woman was killed, while three people suffered life-threatening injuries and eight others were seriously hurt, according to Berlin's fire service. Dobrindt said at least 29 people were injured.

The attack happened a few hundred yards from Berlin's annual Christopher Street Day Pride celebration — one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ events — but not on the parade route or at the festival's closing event near the Brandenburg Gate. Investigators said the victims appeared to include both Pride attendees and other people who were in the park.

Organizers stopped the celebration shortly after the attack, cutting off a live performance and urging people to leave the area.

SYNAGOGUE IN LONDON TARGETED IN ATTEMPTED 'ANTISEMITIC HATE CRIME,' UK POLICE SAY

Police spokesman Florian Nath earlier said the suspect was known to investigators because of his alleged ties to Islamic groups in Berlin.

"The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed," Nath said, according to The Associated Press. "We still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself."

Police searched several locations across Berlin overnight and into Sunday, including an apartment in the Schöneberg district. It was not immediately clear where the confrontation happened.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Self-dressing clothes could help older adults
item.description: KAIST and Stanford researchers built soft robotic tubes into fabric that use air pressure to guide clothing into place in about 10 seconds flat.
item.content:encoded:
Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shirt surprisingly difficult, while balance problems can turn a simple pair of pants into a real challenge. That is what makes a new invention from South Korea's KAIST and Stanford University worth watching.

Researchers have created self-dressing clothes with soft, air-powered robots built into the fabric. Once activated, the garment moves along the body and helps guide itself into place, even while the wearer moves. The technology remains an early research project, but it shows how future clothing could help older adults get dressed with less assistance and stay independent at home longer.

Getting dressed ranks among the basic activities that often determine whether someone can live independently. When mobility or dexterity declines, people may need a spouse, family member or professional caregiver to help with a deeply personal routine.

The researchers behind the project say dressing challenges can reduce autonomy and increase reliance on caregivers. They designed the system for people with limited mobility, including older adults and those recovering from injuries. Stanford researchers have also identified dressing assistance as an important use for future home robots. The university says assistive technology could help older adults remain in their homes as caregiving needs increase.

Dressing requires more movement than many people realize. You need to reach behind your body, lift your arms and shift your weight while handling fabric. Arthritis may make gripping or pulling clothing painful. Meanwhile, shoulder problems can limit your reach. Recovery from hip or knee surgery can also make bending difficult.

Balance adds another concern. Pulling on pants often requires someone to stand briefly on one leg or bend toward the floor. For a person who already feels unsteady, that familiar routine can become stressful. Self-dressing clothes could eventually reduce some of that reaching and pulling. However, researchers still need clinical studies to learn how well the system works for people with real mobility limitations.

The researchers call their system SWAG, which stands for Self-Wearing Adaptive Garment. Instead of placing a large robotic arm next to the person, the team built flexible robotic tubes into the clothing. Air pressure causes these soft structures to unfold and grow along the body.

The movement turns the garment inside out as it advances. That approach allows the clothing to follow the person's shape while reducing friction between the fabric and skin. Think of ivy growing around a wall or tree. The plant advances from its tip rather than dragging its entire length forward. The soft robot uses a similar motion, which helps it follow curves and move across different surfaces.

The idea began when KAIST postdoctoral researcher Nam Gyun Kim was riding his bike when it began to rain. As he kept moving, he wondered how helpful it would be if a raincoat could put itself on.

That simple idea led to a much bigger thought. Instead of making your body do all the pulling, reaching and twisting, what if the clothing could move into place on its own? From there, Kim and the research team began developing garments that use soft robotics to help dress the person wearing them.

Kim says putting on a full suit takes about 10 seconds. The published paper provides additional timing from individual demonstrations. A jacket moved into place in about 13 seconds, while the pants demonstration took roughly 21 seconds. A sleeve prototype took about 14 seconds.

The researchers tested sleeves, jackets and pants. Their results showed that the garments could unfold along the body while keeping contact forces within the team's safety limits. The system also relies on its physical design instead of a complicated control program. That could eventually help simplify the hardware needed for dressing assistance.

Many existing dressing robots use rigid mechanical arms. Those systems must handle loose fabric while carefully avoiding uncomfortable contact with the person. They may also require the person to hold a fixed pose while the robot completes the task. That setup could feel awkward inside a bedroom or bathroom.

The KAIST and Stanford design takes a different approach by placing the robotic mechanism inside the garment. The clothing becomes the helper. Because the system uses soft materials, it can bend around the body rather than approaching it with a hard mechanical structure. KAIST says this design reduces physical strain and supports safer contact.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

Older adults and people with disabilities represent a major potential use for the technology. KAIST also sees possibilities for rehabilitation patients who need temporary assistance after an injury or medical procedure. However, industrial workplaces may adopt the idea sooner.

Semiconductor employees frequently put on protective cleanroom clothing. Emergency workers may also need to suit up quickly while carrying other equipment. The researchers believe air-powered garments could help people put on protective clothing without relying heavily on their hands. The published study also discusses possible medical uses, such as helping healthcare workers apply protective coverings or compression bandages. Those applications remain potential future directions.

The current system remains a research prototype connected to a pneumatic base station. Researchers have yet to announce a consumer price or release date. Several everyday questions remain unanswered. The garments would need to fit different body shapes and movement patterns. Designers would also need to address washing, storage and portable air power.

The research team says future versions may use adjustable sheaths or elastic materials to fit a wider range of bodies. The researchers also want to automate the garment-loading process and improve the controls.

Most importantly, the team says clinical trials involving people with mobility impairments will be essential. Those tests could show whether the clothing feels comfortable and works reliably outside the lab. Researchers also need to explore how the garment comes off. The current work concentrates mainly on dressing, while automated removal remains a future possibility.

You probably will not find robotic clothing hanging in a local store anytime soon. Yet this research gives us a useful preview of where assistive technology may be heading. For you or someone you care about, the biggest benefit could be control over a private daily routine. Clothing that handles part of the pulling and positioning could make mornings less tiring.

It could also delay the point when someone needs another person present simply to get dressed. That possibility still depends on testing, affordability and a design people feel comfortable wearing.

Self-dressing clothes may sound unusual, but the need behind them is easy to understand. Arthritis, limited mobility or recovery from surgery can make getting dressed frustrating and exhausting. For older adults, a garment that helps guide itself into place could mean more privacy, less reliance on a caregiver and more confidence starting the day. The KAIST and Stanford system still has a long way to go. Researchers need to make it portable, test it with people who have mobility challenges and prove it can work safely in a home. Even so, the idea shows how technology could support independence through something as familiar as the clothes you already wear.
