item.title: 'Shark Tank' star Daymond John says 'you'll be screwed' if you do this when starting a business
item.description: Daymond John reveals his top business advice at Fanatics Fest, explaining why Kevin O'Leary and other entrepreneurs never chase money first.
item.content:encoded:
"Shark Tank" star Daymond John is giving fans some blunt advice on how to be successful in business.

When speaking to Fox News Digital at Fanatics Fest, the 57-year-old businessman shared that to have a successful business, you have to build it around "something that you love."

"If you're starting something that you love, you have to want to do it for free. I always say to kids, you know, you got to get paid for what you'd do for free, you'd be able to sell whatever you would buy. So, any business is a great business. Emptying garbage is a great business if you really love it. If you're doing it just for money though, you'll be screwed. Even Kevin O'Leary, you think he does it for money? No, he just likes complicated structures that manage his downside. But at the end of the day, he likes the chess game."

The reality TV star began working at a young age, developing his entrepreneurial spirit before founding FUBU ("For Us, By Us") in 1992 along with three of his childhood friends.

DIGITAL ENTREPRENEUR CREDITS THE WORLD CUP WITH TEACHING ABOUT SOCCER AND BOOSTING HER MONTHLY INCOME

Now a global fashion brand, the business began with John sewing wool hats and T-shirts himself in his mother's house in Queens, New York.

"First of all, I was frustrated by Timberland, and a couple of other people and brands that 'didn’t make clothes for African Americans,'" he told The Source Magazine. "That was why I initially created FUBU. It was my love of fashion as well and my love for music. And I felt that no longer did we have to have the 'make it and they will come theory' like other designers."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He continued: "I was a designer who actually respected the community I was selling to, and it was fun. It was an exciting time. Hip-hop was young and fresh, and I was just happy to wear the clothes that I was making as well as seeing artists and other people wear the clothes that I was making for them."

WATCH: ‘SHARK TANK’ STAR DAYMOND JOHN SHARES WHAT WILL GET YOU ‘SCREWED’ IN BUSINESS

After turning FUBU into a global fashion brand, John joined the original cast of "Shark Tank" in 2009, alongside Barbara Corcoran, O'Leary, Robert Herjavec and Kevin Harrington.

As a shark, John has invested in a number of businesses, helping entrepreneurs get them off the ground. Some of his most famous investments include Bombas and Bubba's-Q Boneless Ribs.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I always look for the person first — before the idea," he told Inc. about his investing philosophy. "I need to know that they are going to get the right information, and not go off and make mistakes without at least trying to educate themselves. I value an entrepreneur I can get behind and trust because I know they are attempting to move forward in life."

While at Fanatics Fest, a Comic-Con style celebration and immersive sports festival, John told Fox News Digital he was looking forward to experiencing everything the festival had to offer as a fan.

"I haven't gotten to see most of it, but for three years in, I mean, this is nuts, right? It's everything from WWE to UFC, to, of course, all the sports stuff, the signing, the trading, all of the celebrities and the sports people here. I'm just here being a fan myself," he said.

item.title: Hikers face $25,000 fine after off-leash dog barked at grizzly bear on Banff National Park trail
item.description: Video shows a small off-leash dog barking at grizzly Bear 142 on a Banff National Park trail as hikers yell but never leash or pick up the pet.
item.content:encoded:
Two hikers are facing charges after their off-leash dog repeatedly ran toward and barked at a grizzly bear during an encounter in Banff National Park.

The incident unfolded on the Taylor Lake trail, about nine miles south-east of Lake Louise, as Washington residents Brook and Kraig Koski backed away from Bear 142, a well-known female grizzly in the park.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

According to reports, Kraig initially encountered the bear while jogging ahead of his wife on the trail. Brook recorded the roughly 90-second video as the bear slowly followed Kraig, who walked backward while facing it and carrying bear spray.

Meanwhile, their small dog, Lola, ran freely between the hikers and the grizzly, at times barking at the bear.

"Back off!" Kraig can be heard yelling.

"You’re too close!" Brook says from behind the camera.

The hikers also repeatedly call for Lola, but at no point in the video do they appear to leash the dog or simply pick her up — despite having ample opportunity to do so.

It’s one of the most frustrating videos you’ll ever watch.

Eventually, Bear 142 leaves the trail and disappears into the woods. The encounter fortunately ended without anyone being injured, but Parks Canada wardens were able to identify the hikers after the video was posted online and racked up millions of views.

WILDLIFE PHOTOGRAPHER STAYS ICE-COLD AS MASSIVE BROWN BEAR WALKS RIGHT UP TO HIS CAMERA

The pair now face regulatory charges under the Canada National Parks Act for having an off-leash dog in a national park. Pets are required to be secured on a leash no longer than three meters, and the hikers could face fines of up to $25,000 if convicted.

"Failure to keep your pets leashed in the national parks poses risks to pets and wildlife," Parks Canada spokesperson James Eastham said in a statement. "Bears and other wildlife may react aggressively toward dogs they view as threats, resulting in their injury or death."

Nick de Ruyter, program director of WildSmart for the Biosphere Institute of the Bow Valley, praised Parks Canada for filing charges because "there was so much time in the video to grab the dog and put it on a leash."

"The safety of them, their pets and other people is far more important than getting that video," he said.

Exactly.

As someone who hikes with my dog all the time, this is the kind of behavior that makes responsible dog owners want to pull their hair out.

Keeping a dog leashed in bear country is not an arbitrary rule designed to ruin anyone’s fun. It protects the dog, the wildlife and every other hiker who may encounter an already-agitated animal farther down the trail.

Instead, Lola was allowed to run around barking at a grizzly while her owners repeatedly yelled her name and continued filming.

This is how dogs get banned from trails. It's how responsible owners who follow the rules end up losing access.

"Off-leash dogs can also cause wildlife stress, leading to them avoiding important habitats and sources of food," Eastham said. "Always keep your pets on leash when visiting national parks."

Bear 142 is estimated to be approximately 16 years old and is the daughter of Bear 122, better known as "The Boss." She has raised several cubs in Banff National Park and lost one earlier this year after it was struck and killed by a train.

Grizzly bears are considered a threatened species in Alberta.

In this case, the hikers were fortunate. The dog was fortunate. And Bear 142 was fortunate that an entirely avoidable encounter did not end much worse.

item.title: ROBERT MAGINNIS: The Pentagon's plan to seize Iran's uranium isn't a raid. It's an invasion
item.description: The Pentagon reportedly revived a plan to send thousands of troops into Iran to seize enriched uranium, but the mission's risks echo Operation Eagle Claw.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon has reportedly revived an extraordinary option for President Donald Trump: Send thousands of American troops deep into Iran to seize enriched uranium from damaged and buried nuclear facilities, according to a new report.

It is being described as a raid. It would be nothing of the sort.

This would be a temporary invasion of hostile territory, launched without real surprise, against an enemy that has spent months expecting us, at sites whose defenses and contents remain uncertain. American troops might seize the objective only to become trapped in a mission with no reliable timetable and no clean exit.

TRUMP SEEKS $672M TO STOP IRANIAN NUKES AS NEGOTIATORS WEIGH FATE OF URANIUM STOCKPILE

The historical parallel is Operation Eagle Claw, the failed 1980 attempt to rescue American hostages in Tehran. President Jimmy Carter had exhausted diplomacy and sanctions after a hostage crisis that had humiliated the United States for six months, as mounting political pressure pushed him toward a complex rescue operation.

It ended at Desert One, where mechanical failures and a collision between a helicopter and a transport aircraft killed eight American servicemen before the rescue force ever reached Tehran.

US MILITARY IS POWERFUL ENOUGH TO CRUSH ENEMIES, BUT CAN IT DEFEAT THEIR 'FINAL 10%?'

Today's military is far more capable, with mature special operations commands and decades of combat experience. But technology does not repeal geography, logistics or enemy action, and a president's need for a decisive result does not make a fragile plan sound.

Trump has shown the Carter analogy concerns him. When asked in June about a uranium-seizure mission, he said he considered it early and rejected it. "I didn't want to be Jimmy Carter," he said.

The reported mission would dwarf Eagle Claw in complexity. Carter's force knew roughly where the hostages were. In Iran today, we may not know precisely where the enriched uranium sits, whether it has been divided among sites, or whether Iran has already moved it. Some officials believe international inspectors have not verified its location in nearly nine months.

The Pentagon plan reportedly contemplates securing Iran's Fordow and Isfahan facilities, along with the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain complex near Natanz, where Iran is believed to have moved centrifuges.

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

Thousands of troops could be required, including Army Rangers, special operations forces and combat engineers. One version reportedly calls for flying in excavation equipment and building a runway to fly out roughly 450 kilograms of highly enriched uranium, some enriched to 60 percent.

Pickaxe Mountain alone shows the scale of the problem. Analysts believe it sits more than 300 feet underground, deeper than the Fordow plant the U.S. struck last year. Open-source evidence does not place uranium there at all; the mountain may hold centrifuges instead, and American forces could fight their way inside only to discover the objective had already disappeared.

Iran knows the likely targets and has spent months preparing entrances, roads and defenses. At Isfahan, tunnel entrances believed to hold much of Iran's enriched uranium reportedly remain backfilled with dirt, reinforced with mines and roadblocks to complicate any ground approach. As one former National Security Council official noted, the sites are fixed and both sides know which facilities American forces would likely approach.

American aircraft might suppress Iran's air defenses and deliver an assault force. That is only the first step. Troops would then have to control roads, tunnel portals and an airfield for heavy cargo aircraft, while engineers bring in heavy equipment and other troops secure a wide perimeter. Inside, they could confront collapsed concrete, mines, poor ventilation and armed defenders in confined passages. Every hour favors Iran.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps would likely respond on multiple fronts: striking American bases, disrupting shipping through Hormuz and activating proxies in Iraq, Syria and Yemen. Tehran would not need to defeat American forces outright, only deny them the objective by collapsing tunnels, contaminating the site or trapping personnel inside.

The longer our forces remain, the more dangerous the mission becomes. What began as a raid becomes a defended American lodgment hundreds of miles inside Iran. The moment American engineers begin building an airstrip on Iranian soil, the raid becomes an invasion.

That raises the question Washington should ask before sending a single soldier underground: Why not deny access to the facilities rather than occupy them?

If the uranium is trapped inside damaged tunnels, the wiser course may be to collapse every known entrance and access route, then maintain surveillance and strike any effort to reopen the site. Iran might carve a concealed entrance or move the material first — but seal, monitor and re-strike may be far more sustainable than sending thousands of Americans into an underground maze.

The goal should be making reopening slow, visible, costly and vulnerable to another strike, not pretending the mountain can never reopen.

Washington should keep demanding International Atomic Energy Agency access and verified accounting of the material as the price of any further relief, paired with sanctions, interdiction and verified international custody of the stockpile.

Trump is not Carter, and this is not 1980. But both presidents confronted an adversary that refused to yield and mounting pressure to deliver one dramatic operation that could break the stalemate. I will not call Trump desperate; that claims knowledge of his state of mind outsiders lack. But the administration plainly faces pressure to convert tactical success into a visible strategic victory, and seizing Iran's uranium for display in American custody would offer precisely that image. Wars punish leaders who confuse a powerful image with a durable outcome.

Wars are not won by counting targets destroyed, but by producing a durable political outcome. American forces have punished Iran and badly damaged its military, but an open-ended ground commitment could still turn success into failure.

Before proceeding, the administration owes the country answers: Do we know where the uranium is? Can we reach it? How many troops are needed to hold the perimeter? What happens when Iran counterattacks? And before placing thousands of Americans on Iranian soil, has Washington secured the legal authority and public support for a ground war?

Most importantly, how do we get our troops home?

Desert One failed before the rescue force reached Tehran. A uranium-seizure mission could reach the mountain, breach the tunnels and still fail because getting in is not the same as getting out. The real test is not whether America can reach the objective. It is whether the objective justifies the cost when a less dangerous strategy may achieve the same strategic result.

item.title: Missing Grand Canyon hiker, 83, rescued after getting separated from companion
item.description: Gerald Guinn, 83, waved from steep terrain after a cellphone ping narrowed the search area, but rescuers faced a grueling overnight carry-out mission.
item.content:encoded:
An 83-year-old hiker who vanished in a remote stretch of Grand Canyon National Park after separating from his companion was found alive after an intense all-night search across rugged burn-scarred terrain, officials said Thursday.

Gerald Guinn, an experienced outdoorsman from Kanab, Utah, was found around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday during a National Park Service helicopter search, about 2.5 miles from where he was last seen on the park's North Rim, according to the National Park Service and the Kane County Sheriff's Office.

Guinn disappeared Monday after he and his hiking companion intentionally split up while taking a short hike around 12:30 p.m. in search of a nearby historic object in a remote area near the park's northeastern boundary, the sheriff’s office said. While his hiking partner found the object, Guinn never showed up. After several hours of searching, the other hiker called for help.

SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR AUSTRALIAN WOMAN WHO VANISHED AFTER SENDING MESSAGE ABOUT GOING FOR A HIKE NEAR LAS VEGAS

Search crews from Grand Canyon National Park, Coconino County Search and Rescue , and Kane County Search and Rescue spent the night looking for Guinn. Teams searched on foot through burned forest, the sheriff’s office said, while drones, search dogs and helicopters helped cover the remote area.

On Tuesday, investigators were able to narrow the search after receiving a cellphone ping from Guinn's phone. When a National Park Service helicopter later spotted him, Guinn waved to the crew overhead, the sheriff's office said.

The helicopter couldn't land because of the steep, rugged terrain, so a Kane County Search and Rescue team hiked about 1.5 miles to reach him. Deputies said Guinn was in good spirits but was cold and unable to walk. Rescuers gave him water and warm clothing while deciding how to get him out safely.

FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT

With darkness setting in, a helicopter rescue was no longer an option. Instead, a paramedic was flown to the scene, and about 20 rescuers took turns carrying Guinn through the rough terrain in a rescue stretcher, clearing fallen trees and marking hazards along the way until they reached a nearby road around 1:30 a.m. — a day and a half after Guinn first set out on the hike.

Guinn was checked by emergency medical personnel and released, according to the sheriff's office.

The National Park Service thanked Coconino County Search and Rescue and Kane County Search and Rescue for helping bring the search to a successful end.

item.title: Meet the terrifying monsters in Christopher Nolan's blockbuster 'The Odyssey'
item.description: From Polyphemus the Cyclops to Calypso the nymph, here are the mythological creatures that define Odysseus' journey in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
item.content:encoded:
Viewers of Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" may be surprised by how many mythological creatures are packed into Homer's ancient epic.

Filled with A-list stars, the major box-office hit takes audiences from one mythical encounter to the next as Odysseus fights to make it home.

"The movie is visually stunning. It needs to be seen in the theater," said Joel P. Christensen, provost and senior vice president for academic affairs at the CUNY Graduate Center and a professor of classics.

EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND

Christensen, a Homer scholar, told Fox News Digital that audiences don't need to read "The Odyssey" beforehand because Nolan provides enough context to follow the story.

Unlike many modern blockbusters with a single central villain, nearly every stop on this journey brings a new monster or supernatural threat.

As Christopher Nolan's adaptation introduces new audiences to the ancient epic, here's a look at the legendary creatures that define Odysseus' journey in the book, according to Encyclopedia Britannica.

Spoiler alert: Plot details from "The Odyssey" are noted below.

The most famous of the Cyclops, Polyphemus traps Odysseus and his crew in his cave before devouring several of the men.

The name Polyphemus roughly translates to "rich in songs and legends" or "widely talked about," per Britannica.

ANCIENT PALACE DISCOVERY CHALLENGES THE MYTH BEHIND SPARTA'S RISE TO POWER

Odysseus eventually blinds Polyphemus with a sharpened wooden stake — allowing him and his remaining crew to escape the Cyclops' cave.

Polyphemus is one of the sons of Poseidon — prompting the sea god to curse Odysseus' journey home.

In the film, Polyphemus is played by actor Bill Irwin.

Laestrygonians are giant cannibals who destroy nearly all of Odysseus' fleet after luring the ships into their harbor.

They appear in Book 10 of "The Odyssey," where they destroy nearly all of Odysseus' fleet at the harbor of Telepylus, hurling massive boulders.

TEEN STUMBLES ON MYSTERIOUS COIN FROM LEGENDARY CITY, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS OVER ITS JOURNEY

Odysseus escapes the attack aboard his lone remaining ship, sailing on to the island of the sorceress Circe.

A powerful sorceress, Circe encounters Odysseus and his crew on the island of Aeaea.

The daughter of Helios, the sun god, Circe famously turns Odysseus' men into pigs but fails to curse the protagonist himself.

She eventually falls in love with the Greek hero and helps him continue his journey home, advising him about the dangers of the voyage ahead.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS EXCAVATE ANCIENT WORKSHOP WITH UNFINISHED SCULPTURES ON GREEK ISLAND

Christensen told Fox News Digital that the most "unforgettable sequence" is when Circe turns Odysseus’ men into pigs — something that may disturb viewers.

"It makes audiences viscerally uncomfortable: It is well paced, imaginative and unsettling," he said. "That’s not strictly a creature scene, but it shows men revealed as creatures!"

Samantha Morton plays Circe in the Nolan film.

In Greek mythology, sirens are half-bird and half-woman creatures who lured sailors to their deaths.

In Book 12 of "The Odyssey," the sorceress Circe warns Odysseus about the Sirens' irresistible song.

COLOSSAL TOMB TIED TO ALEXANDER THE GREAT REVEALED BY OFFICIALS: 'UNIQUE AND MAGNIFICENT'

To protect his crew, Odysseus orders their ears plugged with beeswax while he has himself tied to the ship's mast so he can hear the song without obeying the Sirens.

Scylla and Charybdis are two of the most famous sea monsters in "The Odyssey," presenting Odysseus with one of the most dangerous challenges of his journey home.

In the book, Scylla and Charybdis trap Odysseus in a narrow strait, with Scylla waiting on one side to snatch sailors from passing ships and Charybdis creating a massive whirlpool on the other.

LONG-LOST SANCTUARY TO GREEK GOD DISCOVERED BY ARCHAEOLOGISTS: 'LARGER THAN LIFE'

Odysseus survives by following Circe's advice to sail past Scylla, despite knowing the monster will claim six of his men. 

The move allows him and the rest of the crew to escape.

Calypso is a nymph that Odysseus encounters on the mythical island of Ogygia.

In the book, she falls in love with Odysseus and refuses to let him leave, keeping the Greek hero on the island for years.

Calypso reluctantly lets him go when Zeus orders his release, helping him build a raft to continue his journey home.

Charlize Theron plays Calypso in the film.

Like any adaptation of a sprawling ancient epic, Nolan's film condenses parts of Homer's story for the big screen, Christensen noted.

While visually stunning, the expert said the film's adaptation of some mythological figures falls short of Homer's original.

He pointed to changes in the portrayals of Polyphemus and Circe, arguing that the film makes the Cyclops "more of a monster than a man," while depriving Circe of agency.

Nolan "impl[ies] that she turns men into pigs because she has been sexually assaulted before," said Christensen.

"This is one of the film's weaknesses: Traditional gender roles become a shorthand for actual story."

"Nolan had to reduce some of the repetitions we see in the Homeric ‘Odyssey’ and had to limit the length of some scenes," he said. "He also made the choice to limit the depiction of the divine."

Even so, many of the epic's most recognizable mythological figures remain central to the story.

"For people who do know ‘The Odyssey,’ remember that film is a very different medium than epic poetry is: It is shorter and visual, so many changes are required to allow the story to work as a movie," he said. 

"This is Nolan’s ‘Odyssey,’ not Homer’s."

item.title: Christian school chaplain wins settlement after firing over LGBTQ sermon
item.description: Rev. Bernard Randall was fired, reported to Prevent and blacklisted after preaching on freedom of conscience at Trent College over LGBTQ ideology.
item.content:encoded:
A school chaplain in the United Kingdom who was fired and blacklisted after preaching a sermon on LGBTQ issues has reached a confidential settlement with his former employer, ending a seven-year legal battle.

The Rev. Bernard Randall, an ordained Church of England minister, worked for five years as chaplain at Trent College, an independent school for K-12 students in Derbyshire, England. In 2018, Randall grew concerned when the school partnered with Educate and Celebrate, an outside group whose stated goal was to "smash heteronormativity" and embed queer theory in school culture. The group has since dissolved.

"I objected to [it] at the time it started, and tried to discuss it with the senior leadership, [but] they weren't interested," Randall told Fox News Digital.

The following year, a student asked Randall why pupils were required to accept LGBTQ ideology at a Christian school. Randall said that question, along with similar concerns raised by other students and staff, prompted him to deliver a sermon on freedom of belief and conscience.

CHRISTIAN COP IN UK SUSPENDED FOR ASKING QUESTIONS ABOUT ISLAM DURING DEI TRAINING WINS SETTLEMENT

In his chapel address, Randall told his young students they were entitled to hold traditional Christian beliefs on marriage and biological sex, while emphasizing that they must show respect to those with whom they disagree.

Days later, school administrators summoned Randall to a meeting, interrogated him, suspended him and launched an investigation. He was also reported to local law enforcement and Prevent, the U.K. government's counterterrorism program. Prevent ultimately determined he did not pose a terrorist threat.

In addition, the Diocese of Derby blacklisted Randall as a safeguarding risk to children.

Trent College eventually fired Randall for gross misconduct. He was reinstated on appeal, but under strict conditions that restricted his sermon topics and required prior administrative approval for chapel content. Furloughed during the pandemic, Randall was ultimately made redundant, or laid off, on Dec. 31, 2020.

CARRYING A BIBLE IN NORTHERN IRELAND HOSPITALS COULD BE A CRIME UNDER ABORTION BUFFER ZONE LAWS

Randall challenged his dismissal with the support of the Christian Legal Centre. Following an initial employment tribunal ruling against him, the Employment Appeal Tribunal set aside the judgment, ordered a full retrial and required Trent College to pay £20,000 in costs. Shortly thereafter, Randall and Trent College reached a confidential settlement.

After seven years being barred from ministry, an independent Church of England review conducted by the Diocese of London finally cleared Randall of all safeguarding allegations, ruling the concerns were "unsubstantiated" and finding no evidence of harm.

In a statement shared by his legal team, Randall said he was relieved by the ruling but said that nothing could replace the seven years he's lost from being shut out of ministry.

"I encouraged pupils to think, to debate, and to love their neighbors whatever they believed. No minister, teacher or chaplain should be punished for upholding Christian teaching in a Christian setting," Randall said.

Randall told Fox News Digital he was deeply troubled by the Church of England’s handling of his case, noting that officials spent years disciplining him for teaching orthodox church doctrine.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

"The people who should support you most are the ones doing you harm," Randall said.

He added that standing up for freedom of speech and belief was worth the personal toll. "It's as Jesus said, what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses his soul? And I sort of feel I'm in that position that it matters to stand up and be counted and tell the truth. And that was more important than just an easy, comfortable life."

Randall also voiced broader concerns about the future of free speech in the United Kingdom.

"Oh, I do worry," he told Fox News Digital. "There are groups that are fighting back, and we're not going to let them roll over us. But there are times when I wish we had the First Amendment."

"I think most people in Britain still value free speech," he added. "It used to be in this country, when somebody said something that we thought was a bit strange or odd, [we'd say], 'Oh well, it's a free country.' I don't hear people saying that anymore."

Vice President JD Vance criticized growing restrictions on speech in the U.K. while visiting Munich last year. The U.S. State Department has also raised concerns over the prosecution of peaceful religious expression under British buffer zone laws.

"I know that our American cousins and the people in the White House are looking at Britain and raising the question of free speech, and in Europe too as well," Randall continued. "That has to be a good thing because it doesn't hurt to have our friends from across the Atlantic offer a bit of advice about why it matters that free speech is so important and freedom of conscience, that these things really, really matter. So yes, I'm worried, but I'm not without hope."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

While Randall has completed mandatory safeguarding training and is eligible to return to public ministry, he is waiting for the bishop of Derby, Libby Lane, to grant him permission to officiate, according to The Christian Legal Centre.

Fox News Digital reached out to Trent College for comment.

A spokesperson for the Diocese of Derby told Fox News Digital, "The Diocese is happy to continue supporting Dr Randall’s potential return to ministry as he decides whether and where to apply for a role. Over the past few months, through our ongoing contact with him, he has been signposted to current vacancies in the Diocese of Derby, the Church of England’s 'Pathways' recruitment portal, and to the Church’s Clergy Transitions Service which has confirmed that they are also available to provide further assistance."

Fox News' Jon Brown contributed to this report.

item.title: Clint Black says Billy Joel's 'Uncle Daddy' warning changed his life
item.description: Clint Black reveals how a Billy Joel interview about being an "Uncle Daddy" reshaped his approach to fatherhood after welcoming daughter Lily.
item.content:encoded:
When Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black welcomed their only child, Lily, in 2001, the country star made fatherhood his top priority to avoid becoming an "Uncle Daddy."

Black opens up about that decision in his new memoir, "Killin' Time," named after his triple-platinum 1989 debut album. The Grammy winner reflects on his upbringing, his meteoric rise to fame and a career that has included more than 20 million records sold.

The 64-year-old singer told Fox News Digital he came across an interview with Billy Joel, and the "Piano Man" singer's words stayed with him.

CLINT BLACK AND LISA HARTMAN BLACK'S ONE RULE THAT HAS KEPT THEIR MARRIAGE STRONG FOR NEARLY 35 YEARS

"I saw an interview with Billy Joel, and he was talking about being gone too much. He said he'd come home... and he called it being 'Uncle Daddy,'" said Black. "That was long before we knew we wanted a child, but I remember it sticking with me."

In "Killin' Time," Black recalled Joel saying life on the road often left him feeling more like an "Uncle Daddy" than a father. The comment stayed with Black for years and ultimately reshaped how he balanced his career and family.

"I didn't cut out activities completely when Lily was born," said Black.

WATCH: CLINT BLACK EXPLAINS WHY HE REFUSED TO BE AN ‘UNCLE DADDY’

"I did about 15 shows a year just to take care of the band and crew members.... I read a book or two, and I can't remember which one, but the author was talking about secure attachment for a child — who the child feels is their secure attachment, the person they look to in moments of fright. And if you want to be a secure attachment for your child, it's something you earn in the first three years of their life."

"So that was the number," he continued. "Three years of mostly being home, only going out and doing these small bits of work. I did some work at home, working on music... but I was around to be a dad. It wasn't great for my career, but I wouldn't change a thing. I wouldn't trade a better career for that attachment or the closeness I have with my daughter."

For Black, fatherhood came after years of heartbreak. In the book, he revealed that he and the former "Knots Landing" actress suffered four pregnancy losses before welcoming Lily.

"Trying to have a baby was not something that we had set out to do," he said. "And then, at one point, we realized we had better talk about this and find out where we both stood. And once we decided we wanted to have a child, we really, really wanted to have a child. So when we ran into problems with the miscarriages, it started to hurt. But we kept our hopes up."

"It was still scary getting through it," he admitted. "It wasn't smooth sailing, but it was sailing. We have a 25-year-old daughter now, and she is just a joy."

Black said that when Lily was born, he embraced fatherhood without hesitation.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I think the biggest lesson I've learned from fatherhood is — I'm tempted to say patience — but I don't think that's it," he explained. "I think it's that I can do a lot more than I thought I could. I could have a career, travel, do all of that, come home, be active as a dad, go to basketball practice, volleyball games and school events."

"Taking her to bouncy playhouses, [watching] 'The Wiggles,' 'Bear in the Big Blue House' and 'Wicked,'" he said with a smile. "All the plays and all that stuff. I wouldn't have thought that I could do it all. But I have, and I've surpassed my own expectations. And that's through devoting myself to her, my wife and being present."

These days, Black is back on the road, and every so often, fans can catch Lily sharing the stage with him.

"I'm still doing 80 to 90 cities a year on tour, taking Lily and Lisa with me at times," he said. "They have toured with me. Those are the best tours."

"It's surprising," he reflected. "I went into fatherhood ready to do whatever it took. But the fear I had was, 'Is this going to be too much? I won't be able to do it all.' But I did."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Even today, Black said he's still in awe when he watches his daughter perform alongside him.

"Watching Lily perform right next to me on stage took me a while to adjust to," he admitted. "For a while, I was just the adoring father. I had to learn to be a guy in the band playing to an audience and enjoy what she’s doing and seeing her perform so well without having that be my focus on stage. I think it becomes distracting to the audience if they’re watching us, and they’re watching me with a shifted focus."

"But seeing her beside me, it's a gift," he added.

item.title: Ryan Fox details how he had to negotiate the Claret Jug onto his flight after Open Championship victory
item.description: Ryan Fox details his hilarious conversation with a gate agent to sneak the Claret Jug onto a commercial flight after winning The Open at Royal Birkdale.
item.content:encoded:
Traveling with one of the most iconic trophies in all of sports isn't as easy as one might imagine. Ryan Fox, the Champion Golfer of the Year, quickly found that out while trying to board a commercial airplane with the Claret Jug after winning The Open at Royal Birkdale.

It goes without saying that the morning after becoming a major champion is a hectic one, and then having to deal with the unavoidable headaches at the airport only adds to the stress levels.

SCOTTIE SCHEFFLER ADDRESSES GROWING RIVALRY BETWEEN RORY MCILROY, BRYSON DECHAMBEAU AFTER THE OPEN

To set the scene on the Monday after Fox's stunning victory, the New Zealander jumped on a plane in Manchester bound for London before jetting back home from Heathrow Airport.

After making it through security with the Claret Jug in a protective case, he arrived at his departure gate and realized that he would have to do some finagling to get the hardware onto the plane as a carry-on as opposed to gate-checking it.

Handing over the oldest trophy in professional golf to a stranger and having them toss it underneath the plane isn't exactly an ideal situation, even for a very short flight from Manchester to the country's capital. During an appearance on 'The Smylie Show,' Fox detailed the conversation he had with the gate agent to 'sneak' the Claret Jug onto the plane as an additional carry-on.

"I meekly got up to the check-in agent with these two boxes and go, 'So, yeah, I've got some special cargo here, is there any chance I can just take these on the plane?'" Fox recalled telling the gate agent. "She goes, 'What's in it?' You know, I'm like, 'The Claret Jug, it's the oldest trophy in golf.' [She says] 'Did you win it?' I'm like, 'Uh, yeah. Can I just take it through?' She's like, 'Yep, no problem.'"

Fox also went on to explain that a number of different travelers recognizing him as he made his way through security likely helped his cause.

To make the already incredibly unique situation even more so, Fox made his way on the plane with the Claret Jug and just so happened to be seated directly behind Cameron Young, who finished runner-up at Birkdale after Fox made birdie on the 72nd hole.
